key_insight: The paper shows that poisoning pretraining data is feasible even in realistic, large-scale settings, not just in controlled sources like Wikipedia. It also highlights that data curation pipelines can fail to filter out harmful poisoned content, making attacks harder to detect and defend against.
problem_solved: This work addresses the challenge of whether pretraining data poisoning can still succeed in heterogeneous, web-scale corpora and under modern data curation pipelines, where prior attacks were tested only in limited settings.
method: Studies poisoning attacks on pretraining data in a more realistic corpus setting with large-scale and heterogeneous data.
Examines how poisoned examples interact with data filtering and curation pipelines.
Demonstrates that harmful behaviors can be introduced into language models through poisoned pretraining data beyond previously assumed constraints.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this raises the bar for dataset security and provenance tracking in pretraining pipelines. It suggests that defenses must account for both the scale of the web and the weaknesses of curation filters, not just obvious bad sources.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing data collection, curation, poisoning insertion, and model pretraining.
An attack-versus-defense flowchart illustrating how poisoned samples bypass filtering.
A comparison chart between controlled sources (e.g., Wikipedia) and real-world heterogeneous corpora.
A warning icon over a large dataset cloud to emphasize scale and risk.
paper_title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
paper_authors: Victoria Graf, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, David Kohlbrenner, Kyle Lo
